newsitem.title: UK: Orange Order calls off N.Ireland parade - BBC.
newsitem.headline: Orange Order calls off N.Ireland parade - BBC.

text.p: The BBC said on Thursday that the Protestant Orange Order had called off a planned parade through the Lower Ormeau Road in Northern Ireland's capital Belfast on Saturday to avoid violence.

Catholic residents had called on thousands of its supporters to descend on the area to block the march, which is staged on the anniversary of a victory more than 300 years ago of Protestant over Catholic forces.
The BBC's report was broadcast as the Protestant group called a a news conference in Belfast.
The BBC quoted an Orange Order statement as saying that it had taken a "serious decision" not to parade down the Lower Ormeau Road, where it faces opposition from Catholic residents.
A packed news conference at an Orange Order lodge at one end of the Lower Ormeau Road awaited confirmation of the report.
The BBC said it had learned of the decision and had a document confirming that such a move had been made.

Earlier on Thursday Orange leaders held talks with police chiefs and a veteran Orange offical, James Molyneaux, a former head of the Ulster Unionist party, the province's biggest pro-British organisation.
The parade is staged annually on the "Glorious 12th", the most hallowed date in the Orange Order's calendar.
It marks a 1690 victory by a Protestant king over an invading Catholic monarch which ensured that a Protestant sat on the British throne.
Last Sunday Northern Ireland erupted into the worst violence for years after an Orange Order parade down the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown.
The Order, which is founded on its Protestant faith and British loyalty has been under intense political pressure to call off Saturday's Belfast parade to avoid further violence.
